title: CampusGroups by Ready Education Sees Record Customer Growth
summary: More colleges and universities are choosing CampusGroups, driven by continued innovation and new features ahead of the fall semester.
body_text: More colleges and universities are choosing CampusGroups, driven by continued innovation and new features ahead of the fall semester. CAMBRIDGE, Mass., July 16, 2026 – Ready Education, provider of the CampusGroups student engagement platform , today announced record first-half growth. New institutional adoption for CampusGroups nearly doubled compared to the same period last year, and new customers included 11 R1 research universities . CampusGroups now supports more than 7 million students across 25+ countries, including 81 leading U.S. research universities, 11 of the 13 Ivy Plus institutions, and more than 25 of the world’s leading business schools. For institutions evaluating student engagement platforms this year, the signal from peers has been clear: schools are consolidating around CampusGroups rather than managing engagement across fragmented or dated tools. Under pressure to demonstrate measurable retention outcomes while simplifying their tech stacks, colleges and universities across every institution type have made the same move. That momentum is backed by record-setting investment in the platform itself. In the first half of the year, Ready Education rolled out new AI-Driven Data Intelligence capabilities , giving administrators earlier visibility into engagement trends so they can intervene before disengagement turns into attrition. Many existing customers have already adopted these tools, a sign that peer institutions aren’t just staying on the platform, but deepening how they use it. Institutions adopting CampusGroups during the first half of the year reflected the diversity of higher education. New customers spanned flagship R1 research universities, private colleges and universities, Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCUs), community colleges, regional and international universities, expanding the company’s global footprint. New customers included Florida State University, Oklahoma State University, University of Washington-Seattle, Lehigh University, North Dakota State University, Virginia Tech, and Hamad Bin Khalifa University. Existing customers also expanded their investment in CampusGroups at record levels. The University of Oklahoma, Seton Hall University, and many others expanded their CampusGroups contracts. Four additional schools within the New York State system also adopted the platform, nearly doubling CampusGroups’ presence across their campuses. Many institutions also broadened their use of CampusGroups by adding AI-Driven Data Intelligence or expanding the platform into additional departments, reflecting a growing preference for consolidating student engagement within a single unified platform. Institutions choosing CampusGroups also join a network of more than 700 peer institutions that share strategies and best practices year-round through Ready Education’s customer community, and in person through the Inspire event series. This year’s Chicago Inspire event drew record attendance, bringing together administrators from across the region to compare notes on engagement and retention strategy. Additional Inspire events are planned in Boston and San Jose ahead of fall semester, giving customers direct, ongoing access to the people at other institutions solving the same problems they are. “Institutions aren’t just choosing a platform. They’re choosing a partner,” said Gary Ambrosino, Chief Executive Officer at Ready Education. “They want proven technology, an experienced team that has spent two decades in higher education, and a community of hundreds of peer institutions sharing what works. That combination is why more colleges and universities continue to choose CampusGroups.” Institutions evaluating their student engagement strategy can learn more about why peer institutions are choosing CampusGroups at readyeducation.com . About Ready Education Trusted by over 700 institutions in 25+ countries, including 75% of the top 20 universities worldwide, Ready Education helps colleges and universities build communities and improve retention through the industry-leading CampusGroups platform and app. From orientation through graduation, students use the app daily to navigate campus life, academics, and services in one unified experience. Institutions understand and act on engagement patterns through interactive dashboards and AI-powered insights that make data accessible to administrative leaders across campus. For more information, visit readyeducation.com . Media Contact Lucie-Kay Desthuis-Francis Ready Education 1-877-588-7508 lucie-kay.desthuis@readyeducation.com

title: Never Too Small, Part 2: The Rise Of The Cyber Ambulance Chasers
summary: A recent class-action lawsuit involving a small steel manufacturer suggests that organizations don’t have to be large to attract plaintiffs’ attorneys.
body_text: Two years ago, several of us wrote that Arlington, Massachusetts wasn’t “too small for cybercriminals” after a business email compromise diverted nearly half a million dollars from a town construction project. The criminals didn’t target a major enterprise or a household brand. They found a small municipality with finite staff and resources and even less financial room for error. A recent class-action lawsuit involving a small steel manufacturer suggests that another assumption is due for retirement: Organizations don’t have to be large to attract plaintiffs’ attorneys, either. The manufacturer experienced a breach of employee HR and benefits information including Social Security numbers, dates of birth, driver’s license information, and health-related data, affecting roughly 5,000 individuals. The intrusion reportedly lasted about two days before it was detected and contained. Within weeks of notifying affected individuals, the company was facing a class-action complaint alleging failures in training, oversight, and cybersecurity safeguards. The window to join the lawsuit just closed in May. The Litigation Floodgates Open Prior to 2017, most data-breach cases failed; unless plaintiffs could show actual misuse or harm (not just exposure), they didn’t have the “standing” to sue. That kept many breach claims out of federal court and limited the class-action pipeline. By 2018, however, after five circuit courts ruled that a substantial risk of future identity theft can satisfy Article III standing in data-breach cases , plaintiffs had a path into federal court even before actual misuse occurred, helping turn cyber incidents into class-action fuel. Data Breach Litigation Is Industrializing The details of this case matter less than what it represents. In 2024, Forrester predicted that by 2025, breach-related class-action costs would surpass regulatory fines by 50%, and that’s precisely what’s happened. More than 3,000 data-breach class actions were filed in US federal courts in 2025 alone, making breach litigation one of the fastest-growing areas of complex litigation. Duane Morris’ 2026 Class Action Review analysis counted more than 1,800 data privacy class-action filings in 2025 — that’s more than 150 per month, up more than 25% over 2024, and more than 200% since 2022. And breaches are no longer the only trigger: Cyber risk firm KYND reports that privacy-related cases have climbed from hundreds per year to more than 2,000 , with small and medium-sized businesses (SMBs) disproportionately exposed because of default website configurations and third-party marketing pixels. Portions of the plaintiffs’ bar (the community of lawyers/firms that bring lawsuits on behalf of plaintiffs) have become almost as systematic as the threat actors themselves — think coat and tie vs. a hoodie. Just as cybercriminals monitor exposed systems and credential theft opportunities, plaintiffs’ firms monitor public breach disclosures, recruit affected individuals, and move quickly when the facts suggest the possibility of cyber negligence. State privacy laws sweeten the economics: California’s Consumer Privacy Act allows statutory damages of $100–$750 per resident per incident, with no proof of actual harm required. Additionally, Coalition’s 2026 Cyber Claims Report found that 72% of privacy claims cited the California Invasion of Privacy Act, a 1967 wiretapping statute now being applied to modern web-tracking tools, with 11% specifically alleging improper data sharing through Meta Pixel . A 5,000-person breach doesn’t need to make headlines to make a business case for a lawsuit. Your Employee Data Is The Target Large enterprises frame breach exposure around customer records, intellectual property, and payment card data. Small organizations may not hold vast customer databases, but they almost certainly maintain payroll, benefits, healthcare, and tax records for every employee. These records are among the most sensitive assets in the organization and, from a litigation perspective, are easier to build a case around than many other categories of data. It should also prompt a rethink of “reasonable cybersecurity.” Most breach complaints allege a failure to implement reasonable safeguards — a standard that frustrates security leaders, because “reasonable” is rarely defined. But resource-constrained organizations don’t need to replicate a Fortune 500 program. The more useful question is whether decisions are risk-based, documented, and defensible. Frameworks like NIST CSF and the CIS Controls matter because they provide a structured way to make — and prove — those decisions. Incidents are now judged not just by what happened but by what an organization can demonstrate it was doing beforehand. This is one reason our Forrester colleague James Plouffe is working on research about what we’re calling minimum viable Zero Trust (stay tuned). What SMBs, Municipalities, And Regional Providers Should Do Now Treat employee data as a crown-jewel asset. HR, payroll, and benefits systems deserve stronger protections than they typically receive. In addition, consider the useful lifecycle of employee data and the personal data of job applicants you collect and have in your possession. Delete what you no longer need to use or retain. Bring HR and finance leaders into incident-response planning before a breach. They will be central to employee communications and organizational recovery. Put security obligations in vendor contracts. Contracts are one of your most underused risk tools. Every vendor agreement should define a security incident, set notification timelines, specify required safeguards, and assign responsibility for incident response, investigation, and communications. The lesson from Arlington, Massachusetts still holds. Small organizations are not too small for cybercriminals. The lesson from the steel manufacturer is that they are not too small for class-action litigation, either. Cyber risk and litigation risk now arrive together. And for organizations with limited budgets, staff, and margin for error, a successful intrusion may be only the beginning of their exposure. title: WA - Kate Hickman
summary: Kate Hickman has been a banker with Western Alliance Bank (WAL), since shortly after the institution first opened its doors in 2003. Currently she serves as Managing Director of Commercial Banking.
body_text: Kate Maynard Hickman Managing Director Commercial Banking [email protected] Kate Hickman has been a banker with Western Alliance Bank (WAL), since shortly after the institution first opened its doors in 2003. Currently she serves as Managing Director of Commercial Banking. Kate is well known and respected in the metro Phoenix business community. She was named by Arizona Business Magazine as one of the 2016 Most Influential Women in Arizona Business. The Phoenix Business Journal named her a member of the 40 Under 40 Class of 2016 and in 2017 named her an Outstanding Women in Business. In 2017 she was also named by InBusiness Magazine as a Woman of Achievement. Personally, she is heavily engaged in community giving. Kate is also involved as a board member with Education Forward Arizona, Make-A-Wish Foundation of Arizona and Prisma Community Care. She previously sat on the board of Big Brothers Big Sisters of Central Arizona, Friends of Public Radio Arizona, Support My Club, the Greater Phoenix Chamber, the Arizona Chamber of Commerce and Industry and Ryan House, where she served as vice chair. She is also a former member of the Arizona Technology Council, National Charity League and the Hon Kachina Council. She co-chaired the 2014 Hon Kachina Awards annual ceremony and was an ambassador for the TGen Foundation. Kate holds a Bachelor of Arts in American Studies from the University of Alabama and a minor in history. She lives in Phoenix with her husband and their four children. About Us Western Alliance Bank Western Alliance Bancorporation (NYSE: WAL) is one of the country’s top-performing banking companies and has ranked as a top U.S. bank by American Banker and Bank Director since 2016. Its primary subsidiary, Western Alliance Bank, is a leading national bank for business that puts customers first, delivering tailored business banking solutions and consumer products backed by outstanding, personalized service and specific expertise in more than 30 industries and sectors. With $90 billion in assets and offices nationwide, Western Alliance excels at helping businesses of all sizes capitalize on their opportunities to solve today and succeed tomorrow.

title: Sales intelligence software: What it is and top tools for 2026
summary: Looking for the best sales intelligence software? Learn how native vs. standalone platforms differ and find the right tool to capture 100% of your sales data.
body_text: Your sales team closes a deal, logs off, and moves on to the next prospect. But between that first cold call and a signed contract, hundreds of hours of conversations, messages, and video meetings happened. Most of it was never reviewed. Sales intelligence software exists to change that reality. It transforms raw, unstructured interaction data into actionable business insights. Leveraging the power of AI for sales allows companies to turn these once-hidden interactions into a core engine for growth. The challenge is that most organizations still rely on manual processes, and sales managers can review only about 1% of customer communications at any given time, leaving the other 99% as an untapped, unreviewed blind spot. This guide breaks down what sales intelligence software is, how it works, what to look for, and which platforms are leading the market in 2026. What is sales intelligence software? TL;DR definition Sales intelligence software is a technology platform that collects, analyzes, and distributes data from customer and prospect interactions, including calls, messages, and video meetings, to help sales teams make better decisions, automate administrative tasks, and surface revenue risks At its core, sales intelligence software gives organizations a structured view of what is actually happening in their revenue-generating conversations. It is not a customer relationship management (CRM) system, nor is it a replacement for your broader suite of sales software . Instead, it feeds your CRM with accurate, automatically captured data so that your records reflect reality rather than what a rep remembered to type after a long call. The most important distinction buyers need to understand in 2026 is the difference between traditional point solutions and platform-native software. Most standalone tools operate outside your communication infrastructure. Many rely on external recording bots that join your meetings from the outside, which adds IT overhead, a data security variable, and workflow friction. Some leading standalone platforms also charge annual platform fees on top of per-seat pricing, an expense that comes on top of what you already pay for your communication stack. A modern, platform-native approach is fundamentally different. When sales intelligence is built directly into your communication platform, data is captured automatically across sales, customer service, and business intelligence operations simultaneously. There is no third-party bot. There is no custom integration to maintain. The data flows directly into your existing workflows without any additional setup. This distinction matters because native intelligence protects data hygiene, reduces IT complexity, and ensures that no conversation falls through the cracks because a bot failed to connect. How does sales intelligence software work? Sales intelligence platforms follow a consistent processing loop regardless of which vendor you choose. Understanding this loop helps buyers evaluate whether a platform is truly capturing the full scope of their operations or just scratching the surface. 3-Step Processing Loop Step 1: Data collection and ingestion. The platform captures raw interaction data across every channel where your team communicates: phone calls, video meetings, and messages. On native platforms, this capture occurs automatically within the communication system. For standalone tools, this is where the external bot joins your meetings. Step 2: Automated analysis and scoring. Once data is ingested, the platform applies AI and machine learning models to transcribe, tag, and score the content. It identifies topics, flags risk signals, detects sentiment shifts, and categorizes interactions by outcome, urgency, or deal stage. Step 3: Workflow integration and synchronization. Processed insights are then pushed into the tools your teams already use. CRM records are updated automatically. Managers receive alerts, and AI sales coaching recommendations are delivered to reps based on patterns detected across their calls. for flagged interactions. Executives can query conversation data using natural language to find patterns across the entire business. This three-step loop runs continuously and at scale, which is exactly what makes it more powerful than any manual review process. Core features of modern sales intelligence platforms Most buyers think of sales intelligence as just another entry in their stack of sales enablement tools for their sales development team. That framing is too narrow. Modern platforms extend their value across the full customer lifecycle, including customer service, account management, and post-sale retention. The data trends you miss by limiting visibility to just your sales team are often the ones that predict churn before it happens. Automated database sync and workflow optimization One of the most immediate and measurable benefits of sales intelligence software is the elimination of what operations leaders call the Documentation Tax. This is the systemic drain on productivity that happens when high-value sales reps and customer-facing staff spend hours every week manually typing call summaries, action items, and follow-up notes into their CRM instead of spending that time with prospects and customers. A complete platform removes this burden entirely. After every call or meeting, your AI sales assistant automatically generates a summary, extracts action items, and syncs the full record directly into your CRM. The rep gets off the call and moves immediately to the next conversation. The CRM is updated in the background with accurate, structured data. This is not just a quality-of-life improvement for individual contributors. At scale, it means that leadership is working from an accurate picture of pipeline activity rather than a patchwork of manually entered notes with varying levels of completeness. Interaction risk and signal isolation Here is a reality that most sales leaders already know but rarely say out loud. Your quality assurance team and sales managers do not have the bandwidth to review more than a fraction of recorded calls. In practice, that fraction is less than 1%. The other 99% of customer interactions sit in a storage system, unreviewed, carrying risk signals that no one ever sees. Implementing conversation intelligence is the only way to tap into that 99% and uncover these hidden risks. Think about what lives in that 99%: a customer who mentioned switching to a competitor, a rep who promised a discount that was never approved, a prospect who raised a compliance concern that was brushed aside. Any one of those moments, left unreviewed, can become a revenue leak or a legal exposure. Sales intelligence software acts as a virtual supervisor, automatically processing every interaction. It does not sample. It reviews everything and surfaces only what requires human attention. Managers receive a prioritized feed of flagged moments rather than a list of recordings to manually sift through. By deploying an AI sales agent , teams can automate interaction reviews, take action based on these signals, and ensure no revenue risk goes unaddressed. Risk signals get addressed in hours, not weeks. Strategic observability via natural language Beyond the daily operational benefits, advanced sales intelligence software gives executive leadership something that has historically been impossible to achieve at scale: strategic observability. Traditional feedback loops in most organizations are reactive. Leadership discovers that a product has a problem when a bad review appears online or when a customer escalates to the C-suite. By the time that signal reaches decision-makers, weeks or months of damage have already accumulated. Sales intelligence software closes that gap by allowing executives and operations leaders to query the full body of customer conversations using natural language. Instead of waiting for a quarterly review, a VP of Sales can ask the platform what objections came up most frequently last month, which accounts are showing signs of frustration, or how reps are handling a newly launched feature. This level of revenue intelligence empowers leaders to act on data, not guesses. The answers come from real conversation data, not from survey responses or anecdotal manager reports. This shift from reactive feedback lag to proactive, real-time mastery is what separates organizations that use sales intelligence strategically from those that treat it as a note-taking add-on. The best sales intelligence software platforms of 2026 Before evaluating individual vendors, buyers need to understand that the sales intelligence landscape is split into two fundamentally different operational layers. These layers are not competing with each other. They capture different types of data at different stages of your sales cycle, and the strongest enterprise stacks use both. Prospecting and data enrichment engines are static databases. They are designed to help you map your market before any conversation happens. They find verified contact details, track job changes, monitor buying signals from public data sources, and help you build target account lists. Their data comes from company databases, web scraping, and third-party data providers. Interaction and conversation intelligence engines are active data capture systems. They operate during and after live interactions. They record, transcribe, and analyze actual calls, messages, and video meetings in which your reps engage with prospects and customers. Their data comes from your own communication stack. Platform name Category Where it gets its data Primary operational focus LinkedIn Sales Navigator Prospecting and enrichment LinkedIn network and profile data Account and contact targeting Apollo.io Prospecting and enrichment Proprietary contact database and web data Lead generation and sequencing ZoomInfo Prospecting and enrichment Company and contact intelligence database Market mapping and intent data RingCentral ACE Conversation intelligence Native communication platform data Full-lifecycle interaction analysis Gong Conversation intelligence Meeting and dialer recordings via integrations Enterprise deal intelligence and forecasting Zoom Revenue Accelerator Conversation intelligence Zoom meeting recordings Deal and coaching insights Dialpad AI Conversation intelligence Dialpad call and meeting recordings Call assistance and analytics Prospecting and data enrichment engines LinkedIn Sales Navigator LinkedIn Sales Navigator is the standard for social selling and account-based prospecting. It gives sales teams access to LinkedIn’s full professional network, with advanced filters for targeting by role, company size, industry, and buying committee membership. Its strength is in relationship mapping and identifying warm paths into target accounts. It does not capture or analyze what happens in your actual sales conversations. Apollo.io Apollo.io combines a large B2B contact database with outbound sequencing tools, making it a popular choice for teams that want to manage prospecting and outreach from a single platform. It provides intent data signals and CRM enrichment features to keep contact records up to date. Like all prospecting tools, its visibility ends when the first conversation begins. ZoomInfo ZoomInfo is one of the most comprehensive B2B intelligence databases on the market. It provides detailed firmographic data, technographic insights, and buyer intent signals derived from web activity. Enterprise teams use it to prioritize accounts and identify contacts who are actively researching solutions in their category. Its focus is entirely on the pre-interaction stage of the sales cycle. Interaction and conversation intelligence engines RingCentral ACE RingCentral AI Conversation Expert (ACE) is built natively into the RingCentral communication platform. Because it operates inside the same system your team uses for calls, video meetings, and messaging, it captures interaction data without any third-party bots or external integrations. ACE automatically transcribes and analyzes conversations across sales and customer service operations simultaneously, flags risk signals, automates CRM updates, and enables leadership to query conversation data using natural language. Its native architecture means there is no additional software to manage, no separate login, and no integration to break. Gong Gong is the most established name in dedicated revenue intelligence, with deep deal analytics, forecasting, and AI coaching scorecards built for enterprise sales organizations. It operates as a standalone platform layered on top of your existing meeting and dialing stack, and its pricing reflects its enterprise focus: premium per-seat costs plus annual platform fees, typically on multi-year contracts. Its coverage is centered on sales teams, so organizations looking for visibility across customer service and post-sale interactions will need additional tooling. Zoom Revenue Accelerator Zoom Revenue Accelerator is Zoom’s built-in conversation intelligence layer for teams that run their sales calls primarily through Zoom Meetings. It provides deal tracking, coaching insights, and call summaries for reps and managers. Dialpad AI Dialpad AI offers transcription, live coaching prompts, and post-call summaries for teams using the Dialpad communication platform. It is particularly strong for contact center and customer service use cases. Like other platform-specific tools, its intelligence is tied to interactions that run through Dialpad’s own infrastructure. Which sales intelligence software should you choose? Choosing the right sales intelligence software is a vendor evaluation, not a feature checklist. Platforms that look similar in a comparison table can produce very different outcomes depending on how they integrate with your existing communication stack and how much of your operation they actually cover. Before signing an enterprise contract, challenge every prospective vendor with these four questions. Are we adding separate, disconnected software tools to our existing communication system?Ask your vendor to explain exactly how their platform captures data from your calls and meetings. If the answer involves an external recording bot that joins meetings from the outside, you are adding IT overhead, a new maintenance burden, and a data security variable to your stack. Evaluate whether a native platform for your communication system would eliminate that friction entirely. Is this software just a note-taker for individual reps, or can leadership search all conversations for business trends?Many conversation intelligence tools are designed to help a single rep summarize their last meeting. That is useful, but it is not the same as giving your VP of Sales or Chief Revenue Officer the ability to query the entire body of customer interactions for strategic patterns. Make sure you understand which level of observability the platform actually supports. Are our teams wasting hours manually typing summaries and action items into our CRM?Before evaluating any platform, calculate how much time your reps currently spend on post-call documentation. A complete sales intelligence platform should eliminate that workload entirely by automatically syncing summaries, transcripts, and action items into your CRM after every interaction. If the platform requires manual input to complete the record, it is not fully automated. Does our software only track outbound sales, or does it protect revenue after the deal closes?A signed contract is not the end of the revenue relationship. Customer retention, expansion, and satisfaction all depend on what happens in post-sale interactions. Evaluate whether your platform gives you visibility into customer service conversations, account management calls, and support interactions, not just your sales development team’s activity. Frequently asked questions about sales intelligence software What is sales intelligence software? Sales intelligence software is a platform that captures, analyzes, and distributes data from business conversations, including phone calls, video meetings, and messages, to help sales and operations teams make better decisions, automate CRM updates, and surface risk signals across the customer lifecycle. What is the best AI tool for sales? The best AI tool for sales depends on what stage of the sales cycle you need to cover. For prospecting and lead identification, platforms like ZoomInfo and Apollo.io are widely used. For conversation analysis, CRM automation, and post-sale visibility, a native conversation intelligence platform like RingCentral ACE provides broader operational coverage without the integration overhead of standalone tools. How does sales intelligence software differ from a CRM? A CRM is a database that stores customer records, deal stages, and contact history. Sales intelligence software is the layer that automatically populates and enriches that database. Instead of relying on reps to manually enter notes, sales intelligence platforms capture interaction data directly and sync it into your CRM. They work together rather than as alternatives to each other. How is sales intelligence software typically priced? Most sales intelligence platforms use a per-seat, subscription-based pricing model, billed monthly or annually. Prospecting tools like ZoomInfo and LinkedIn Sales Navigator often charge based on the number of users and the level of data access. Conversation intelligence platforms are typically priced per user per month and may include additional fees for advanced features like executive-level analytics or API access. Enterprise contracts usually include custom pricing based on team size and usage volume. RingCentral ACE gives your team conversation intelligence that is built directly into the platform they already use every day. No bots. No integrations. No blind spots. Explore RingCentral AI Conversation Expert and see how native intelligence changes what your sales data can actually tell you. Updated Jul 21, 2026

title: Blue Bird Featured in 250th U.S. Anniversary Campaign as a Century-Old American Manufacturer
summary: 100 years of building iconic yellow school bus earns Blue Bird a place in the nation’s milestone celebration
body_text: MACON, GA (July 7, 2026) — Blue Bird Corporation (Nasdaq: BLBD), the leader in electric and low-emission school buses, has been selected to participate in a USA Today video series commemorating the 250th Anniversary of the United States. The feature recognizes Blue Bird as a long-standing, iconic American company that has shaped daily life across the country for the past 100 years. “Blue Bird has had the privilege of safely transporting generations of American children to and from school for nearly a century,” said John Wyskiel, president and CEO of Blue Bird. “Being included in the nation’s 250th Anniversary celebration is a tremendous honor that reflects the trust families, schools and communities have placed in us. We remain as committed as ever to building the safest, cleanest and most reliable school buses right here in Georgia.” Founded by Albert Luce, Sr., Blue Bird began manufacturing school buses in 1927 and has spent the decades since defining the modern “yellow” school bus. Over its lifetime, the company has built more than 620,000 school buses, roughly 180,000 of which remain in operation today. Blue Bird is the only U.S.-owned and operated school bus manufacturer with its headquarters in Macon, Georgia, and its manufacturing facility in Fort Valley, Georgia. Safety has been, and will continue to be, central to Blue Bird’s mission. In 2016, the company was first to market with Electronic Stability Control, a feature that enhances safety by preventing rollovers and loss-of-control in poor driving conditions. In 2025, Blue Bird achieved two major industry milestones, making three-point seatbelts standard on every school bus and becoming first to market with driver airbags. Additional safety innovations include high-resolution front and rear cameras, LED headlights for clearer visibility, illuminated school bus signage and stop arms, and high-intensity exterior LED lighting. Beyond making its buses safer, Blue Bird is also improving the air around them through low- and zero-emission school buses. The company produced its first electric bus in 1994 and its first propane bus in 2008. Those early investments have grown into more than 27,000 propane and electric school buses sold, collectively reducing tens of thousands of metric tons of carbon dioxide each year. Acumen Media is proud to be shining a light on Blue Bird’s leadership in this industry and broader efforts to support the American education system, by providing the transportation that allows it to function. Blue Bird will be one of many organizations to feature as a part of Acumen’s celebratory America 250 campaign, charting the growth and successes of American companies. The video aired on July 2, 2026 and can be viewed on the USA Today website . As America reaches the 250 year milestone, Blue Bird celebrates nearly a century of driving the future of school transportation. About Blue Bird Corporation Blue Bird (NASDAQ: BLBD) is recognized as a technology leader and innovator of school buses since its founding in 1927. Our dedicated team members design, engineer and manufacture school buses with a singular focus on safety, reliability, and durability. School buses carry the most precious cargo in the world – 25 million children twice a day – making them the most trusted mode of student transportation. The company is the proven leader in low- and zero-emission school buses with more than 25,000 propane, natural gas, and electric powered buses sold. Blue Bird is transforming the student transportation industry through cleaner energy solutions. For more information on Blue Bird’s complete product and service portfolio, visit www.blue-bird.com .
